name: A Tang 'Sancai' 'Baoxianghua' Box — 唐三彩宝相花粉盒
description: This tricolor (sancai) box has a round shape with shallow straight walls, a concave circular mouth, a flat base, and a slightly curved lid. The outer surface of the lid is decorated with intricate molded patterns, displaying exquisite and varied designs. The exterior of the box is covered in tricolor glazes, including green, yellow, white, and blue. The interior of the box and the base are covered in yellow glaze. The entire piece is adorned with fine crackle patterns. During the mid-Tang Dynasty, the tricolor glazing technique reached its peak, resulting in a wide variety of vessel forms and refined craftsmanship. The glaze colors during this period were lustrous and the coloring appeared natural. Vessels were often fully glazed both on the inside and outside, utilizing colors such as green, yellow, white, blue, and black, creating a complex and diverse palette. The production process involved applying a base layer of slip before adding various colored glazes to achieve the desired overall effect in terms of both form and decoration. The decoration techniques included carving, stamping, appliqué, and modeling. These tricolor artifacts showcased rich content and were considered exquisite examples of Tang tricolor ware.
notes: Period as catalogued: Tang Dynasty 唐

name: A Blue-Glazed Ceramic 'Tiger' — 青瓷虎子
description: This blue-glazed ceramic tiger was crafted during the Three Kingdoms Period and originates from the Yue Kiln. It features a rounded and well-proportioned form with a slanting neck and circular mouth. The abdomen showcases a bow-shaped handle resembling a tiger in motion, with the tiger's head tilted upwards at a 45-degree angle and a round open mouth. The lower abdomen is sculpted to depict contracted limbs. The handle behind the tiger's head is also adorned with delicate lines. The entire piece is covered in a light blue glaze. Another similar piece with the same design measures 15.7cm in height, 20.9cm in length, and has a mouth diameter of 4.8cm. This tiger was unearthed in 1955 in Zhao Shigang, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province. In August 2013, it was listed in the "Third Batch of Cultural Relics Prohibited from Going Abroad (Abroad) for Exhibition" by the National Cultural Heritage Administration. Inscribed on its lower abdomen are thirteen characters: "Crafted by Master Yuan Yi from Shangyu, Kuaiji, in the 14th year of Chiwu." This piece represents one of the earliest known ceramics with an accurate dating inscription discovered through archaeological excavation.
notes: Period as catalogued: Three Kingdoms Period 三国时期

name: A 'Ding' Lotus Petal Pattern Tea Bowl — 定窑莲瓣纹茶盏
description: This tea bowl has a flared mouth, deep curved walls, and a short ring foot. The outer wall is carved with protruding large lotus petal motifs. The interior of the bowl has a ring-shaped unglazed area at the bottom, with a central lotus flower pattern. The tea bowl features a green-yellow glaze, which is thick in texture, and the entire piece is covered with fine crackle patterns.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋  Material as catalogued: Ceramics

name: A 'Jizhou' Black Glazed "Starry Sky" Tea Bowl — 吉州窑黑釉满天星茶盏
description: This tea bowl features a flared mouth, sloping walls, and deep rounded belly with a slightly raised center resembling a flat disk. It has a mock ring foot with a slightly recessed center. The overall shape of the bowl resembles a "douli" hat. The entire surface is covered in black glaze. The interior walls are adorned with nine concentric circles of regular white spots, where the raised areas appear as dark brown circles with central white spots. This pattern resembles stars orbiting the sun. The exterior laze is lustrous, with the white spots cascading down evenly. The foot lacks glaze, and the body is densely covered with crackle patterns.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋

name: A Ge Washer — 哥窑水盛
description: The Ge washer embodies a round body with a slightly flared mouth, gently curved walls, and a narrowing below the mouth that leads to a reclining foot. The contour lines seamlessly blend gentle curves with subtle straight edges, creating an elegant and harmonious aesthetic. Coated with a pinkish-blue glaze, the application is notably lavish, resulting in a luxuriously thick and smooth appearance, reminiscent of solidified cream. This lustrous surface exudes a radiant and precious quality, with numerous bubbles forming within the glaze, evoking the appearance of hidden pearls. This distinct feature came to be known as the "concentrated foam gathering pearls" effect among connoisseurs. The glaze on the lip of the washer appears slightly whiter, akin to the hue of jade, and gradually deepens in color towards the lower portion. The entire surface is adorned with closely packed fine crackles, imparting a sense of tranquility and antique elegance. Deeper areas of the glaze exhibit a rich brown hue, while shallower sections take on a captivating golden-yellow shade. The interplay between these varying depths of color creates an exquisite and harmonious "golden thread iron wire" effect.
notes: Period as catalogued: Late Ming/Early Qing Dynasty 明晚期/清早期  Catalogued period spans two dropdown options; the earlier option was selected.

name: A Yellow-Glazed Flat Vase — 黄釉胆式扁瓶
description: This flask has a flat body, resembling a leather water bag. The flat mouth slightly flares out, the long and flat neck widens towards the belly, which is shaped like a hanging gall bladder. The bottom features a concave foot. Both the interior and exterior are coated with yellow glaze. The glaze color transitions from a light shade near the mouth to a gradually deeper tone towards the lower part. The entire piece is adorned with delicate crackle patterns. Known as "leather bag flask," this form is named after its resemblance to a leather bag for holding water. It is a distinctive ceramic vessel of the Khitan ethnic group during the Liao Dynasty. The Khitans were a nomadic people of Northern China who used leather water bags, and after settling down, they created many ceramic vessels that imitated the form of leather bags. The flask has a flat body, straight sides, and a rounded lower part. Lines resembling stitched leather seams are created on both sides of the flask. At one end of the mouth, there is an upright short spout. These ceramic vessels were often coated with green glaze and are frequently found in Liaoning and Inner Mongolia. Some are made of white porcelain and date to the early Liao Dynasty, while others are covered in yellow glaze and were intended for imperial use. In the early period, the flask had a shorter body and a chubby lower part, earning it the nickname "mǎ dēng hú", meaning "stirrup flask," due to its resemblance to a horse's stirrup. In the later period, the flask's body became taller, and the stitched seam appearance gradually disappeared.
notes: Period as catalogued: Liao Dynasty 辽

name: A Celadon Twin-Handled Jar — 青釉双系罐
description: This jar originates from the early Western Zhou Period. It features a flared mouth with rounded lips, a short neck, outward-flaring walls, a folded belly, a cinched waist, and a flat base. There is a corded pattern beneath the neck, and on each side, there are twin horizontal handles. Both the interior and exterior of the jar are coated with blue- green glaze, with the glaze flowing down to the bottom like pearls. The color forms a blue ring at the bottom of the jar. The interior glaze creates a bright and vibrant blue color, resembling a gemstone. The jar has numerous dotted raised areas both inside and outside, densely covered with fine glassy crackle patterns. The glaze is clear and translucent, exhibiting a subtle blue hue. The base has a delicate texture. The jar's design resembles a fish trap with its flared mouth and large folded belly, designed to increase its capacity. Primitive celadon first appeared during the Shang Dynasty approximately 3000 years ago. It evolved through the Western Zhou, Spring and Autumn, and Warring States periods into the Han Dynasty. It marks the transitional phase from pottery to porcelain. This jar represents the primary form of early Western Zhou primitive celadon. During this period, the significance of glaze was recognized for its aesthetic appeal, water resistance, and ease of cleaning. The glaze used during this time was a type of glass, and due to the presence of various metal ions, it produced a range of colors when fired at high temperatures
notes: Period as catalogued: Western Zhou Period 西周时期

name: A "Jian" Tea Bowl — 建窑茶盏
description: This tea bowl features an open mouth, deep belly, and shallow ring foot. The body is thick and heavy with a black glaze. The base is inscribed with the characters " Gong Yu " (For Imperial Use). During firing, the glaze flows downwards, creating a mottled yellow-brown color on the rim. The interior and exterior of the bowl exhibit "niu mao zhuang" patterns, resembling delicate strands of cow hair. This effect is akin to a gentle drizzle, rising and falling like wisps of silver waves, caressing the water's surface. The overall glaze is warm and lustrous, and the thick body retains heat exceptionally well. Competitive tea-making involved compressing semi-fermented tea leaves into cakes, grinding them, and then placing them in bowls. Boiling water was poured over the tea, creating a white foam. The abundance and duration of the foam determined the quality of the tea.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋

name: A Lotus-Mouth Celadon-Glazed Bowl — 莲口青釉碗
description: This bowl has a flat rim with six petal-like lobes, a deep curved body, and on the exterior of the rim, there are carved decorations resembling six petal shapes. The flared foot has three circular openings carved in the shape of plum blossoms. The entire piece is coated with sky-blue celadon glaze, with the glaze flowing down from the rim, almost exposing the body. The bowl body and the base are richly coated with glaze, and the body of the bowl is covered with fine crackle patterns. The foot is fully glazed, and three support studs were used during firing. The bowl's form is neat, and the glaze is thick and lustrous. The sky-blue color was highly admired by the Song people and was often achieved by incorporating agate into the glaze. This bowl, being of elegant form, could have been used for ritual purposes. It's worth noting that bowls like this were also used as oil lamps, suspended from a tall stand or carried alongside other offerings during ceremonies.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋

name: A JIAN 'HARE'S FUR' TEA BOWL — 建窑兔毫盏
description: The conical bowl is covered inside and out with a lustrous blackish-brown glaze finely streaked with russet 'hare's fur' markings.
notes: Period as catalogued: SONG DYNASTY (AD 960-1279) 宋 (AD960-1279)

name: A 'Cizhou' White Glazed Black Floral Bowl — 磁州窑白釉黑花钵
description: The globular body set over a low foot and rising to a short upright mouthrim, covered overall in an ivory glaze stopping neatly above the foot and painted in bold black strokes with a foliate scroll wrapping around the shoulder and sides, the unglazed foot a pale buff tone
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋

name: A 'Ding' Incised Fish Plate — 定窑划花双鱼盘
description: This plate has an open mouth, shallow curved body, slender foot, and a circular base with applied foot rim. It underwent single-firing during the kiln process. The entire surface is coated with a white glaze, rendering the outer wall smooth and unadorned. The inner wall is embellished with incised decorations. Two fish are incised and depicted swimming in opposing circles, resembling the movement of Tai Chi, surrounded by wave motifs. The entire scene is lively and dynamic, with the incised fish appearing vivid and lifelike. The wave motifs are finely incised using a comb-like tool,highlighting the intricate details. Ding Kiln was primarily located in Quyang County, Baoding City, Hebei Province, and emerged as a prominent ceramic kiln system after the white porcelain of Xing Kiln during the Tang Dynasty. Ding Kiln thrived during the Northern Song Dynasty and produced porcelain for imperial use. Its products were known for their pure white glaze, earning it the distinction of "Southern Green, Northern White."
notes: Period as catalogued: Southern Song Dynasty 南宋

name: A Longquan Double Phoenix Ear Vase — 龙泉窑双凤耳尊
description: This vase features a flat mouth, a straight neck, flared shoulders, a straight belly, and a circular foot. A phoenix ear is placed on each side of the neck. The overall proportion is harmonious, and the weight distribution is stable. The glaze layer is thick and lustrous, with a serene color tone. The overall design is simple yet elegant, exuding a sense of antiquity. During the Song and Yuan Dynasties, Longquan Kiln switched from using high- calcium lime glaze to low-calcium lime-alkali glaze. This change increased the viscosity of the glaze, preventing it from flowing easily. Influenced by contemporaneous official kiln techniques, multiple layers of glaze were applied, enhancing the jade-like quality and creating high-quality celadon wares. Notably, a Southern Song Dynasty Longquan celadon vase with phoenix ears is represented in the National Palace Museum in Taipei. Archaeological excavations have also revealed similar pieces, such as the Longquan celadon vase with phoenix ears unearthed in 1997 from Chongqing's Kaixian County cellar.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋

name: A 'Ding' 'Jingping' Vase — 定窑净瓶
description: This vase features a slightly raised lip, a slender elongated neck, a melon-shaped body with a raised band, a shallow foot, and a jade-bi style base. The entire body and foot are coated with white glaze, fired on with spur marks. The body is covered with fine crackle patterns, and the belly is adorned with an ink and color painting of cranes and birds. This type of vessel, also known as a long-necked bottle, was popular during the late Tang Dynasty and was used as a ritual vessel for purification in Buddhist ceremonies. Ding Kiln originated and developed during the Tang Dynasty in China, inheriting and evolving the craftsmanship of Xing Kiln. The porcelain body is pure white and fine, while the glaze is glossy and snow-white, and the forms are well-proportioned. Due to the flourishing of Buddhist culture during the Tang Dynasty, Buddhist practices were highly revered, and exquisite white porcelain vessels like the pure white vase became essential ritual items. The long-necked bottle, as a type within the development of pure white vases, served as a ceremonial vessel for ritual purification. Although this specific type of pure white vase is not commonly found, a small number are still preserved in various major museums.
notes: Period as catalogued: Tang Dynasty 唐

name: A Pair of Famille Rose High-Footed Plates — 粉彩高足花口盘（一对）
description: These exquisite pair of high-footed plates feature delicate famille rose painting and are renowned as precious gifts to celebrate blessings. Depicting an auspicious scene of maternal care and education, the plates showcase a woman holding a fan while observing two children at play. The pomegranates at her feet symbolize fertility. One child holds a Sheng (a traditional Chinese wind instrument), while the other holds a lotus, symbolizing wealth, prosperity, and virtuous governance. Behind the woman stands a maid holding a gift voucher, representing a future filled with joyous occasions for the children. The tabletop is adorned with various items, including boxes, scenes, and books, embodying scholarly pursuits, prosperity, and integrity. These high-footed plates, characterized by their meticulous famille rose painting, are a masterpiece of the Republican period, reflecting exquisite craftsmanship and attention to detail
notes: Period as catalogued: Republican Period 民国

name: A Copper-Red Guanyin Vase — 郎窑红观音瓶
description: This exquisite Guanyin vase, reminiscent of ancient bronze shapes, showcases a flared mouth, short neck, rounded shoulders, and an elongated body tapering towards a slightly flared foot. The exterior boasts a rich red glaze, while the interior rim and base are adorned with rice-yellow glaze, creating an elegant contrast. Delicate string patterns grace the neck, enhancing the vivid glaze, reminiscent of glass-like brilliance. Its distinct "niu mao" crackle pattern, akin to cow hair, cascades down the body. The intricately gilded "huiwen" motifs and ruyi symbols on the mouth exterior blend seamlessly with the gilded dragon, phoenix, and flame patterns adorning the body, symbolizing auspicious themes. The gilded wave motif near the foot adds a final touch of detail. This Langyao red vase exemplifies exquisite craftsmanship and artistic sophistication of the Kangxi Period era Langyao red glaze, known for its vibrant color and glass-like luster, flows beautifully during high firing, resulting in an alluring "lamp grass" effect along the mouth rim. The unique two-tiered foot ring technique prevents excessive glaze flow over the foot, contributing to its exceptional appearance.
notes: Period as catalogued: Early Qing Dynasty 清 早期

name: A Copper-Red LaifuZun — 郎窑红莱菔尊
description: This elegant Laifu Zun, resembling ancient bronze shapes, features a flared mouth, slender neck, rounded shoulders, elongated body, and a narrow foot ring. The exterior showcases the iconic Lang kiln red glaze. The mouth rim reveals a thin and sparse red glaze flow, creating a distinctive "lamp grass" effect with a circle of white porcelain called " Deng Cao Kou " ("lamp grass mouth"). The shoulder and neck exhibit three raised string patterns, where the glaze is shallow on the raised parts and flows thicker in the recessed areas, creating a visually striking contrast. The glaze gradually thickens and deepens as it flows down the body, accumulating significantly around the foot, a phenomenon known as " Lang Bu Jin " ("Lang does not flow"). The base lacks glaze and exhibits a finely-textured dry surface. With its flowing lines and balanced proportions, this vessel is a remarkable example of Kangxi Period-era craftsmanship.
notes: Period as catalogued: Qing Dynasty 18th Century 清朝 十八世纪

name: A Longquan Floral Pattern Vase — 龙泉窑花觚
description: This vase features a long neck with a slightly flared mouth, a gently curved neck leading to a round belly with raised string patterns. The belly is intricately carved with floral motifs, and beneath it are raised string patterns. The foot wall gently curves outward. The entire vase is covered with a serene green glaze, exhibiting a rich glaze color. The body of the vase is adorned with abundant crackling. Longquan kiln celadon is named after its primary production area in Longquan City, Zhejiang Province. It reached its zenith during the Three Kingdoms period and flourished throughout the Song Dynasty, culminating in the Qing Dynasty. Longquan kiln celadon boasts a lush green glaze. In the Northern Song Dynasty, it often had a pink blue hue, while in the Southern Song Dynasty, it exhibited a celadon green color. These pieces lacked exposed clay at turning points and frequently revealed the natural color of the clay body. The thick and lustrous glaze was often adorned with applied decorations and relief designs. Longquan kiln celadon products were highly sought after in Asian markets.
notes: Period as catalogued: Qing Dynasty 清代

name: A Famille Rose Yutangchun Vase — 粉彩花卉玉堂春瓶
description: This Yu Tang Chun Vase boasts intricate famille rose decorations depicting elements like grottoes, peonies, chrysanthemums, and bamboo, symbolizing abundance. Orchid patterns grace the lower section, while the upper body showcases four- season floral motifs and cloud patterns. The neck displays pink lotus leaf patterns, "Fu Shou Chang Chun" motifs, and auspicious symbols near the mouth. The base bears the inscription "Da Qing Qianlong Nian Zhi." The Yu Tang Chun vase's elegance, graceful lines, and proportions made it a favorite among Qing emperors. It was designed under Emperor Yongzheng's directive by Tang Ying. These vases were given as rewards for officials promoting clean governance. The Yu Tang Chun vase's form remained unchanged over successive reigns, becoming a quintessential ceramic form of the Qing period. The vase's blue and white intertwined lotus pattern is common, but the famille rose version, like this piece, is exceptionally precious. It features luxurious decorations and intricate paintings. Designs like the "Famille Rose Hundred Bats Yu Tang Chun" and "Famille Rose Hundred Butterflies Yu Tang Chun" emerged. Variations like the "Clear Blue Glaze Yu Tang Chun" appeared in the Guangxu period. In auctions, Qing Qianlong Period blue and white intertwined lotus pattern Yu Tang Chun vases have fetched notable prices.
notes: Period as catalogued: Qing Dynasty 18th Century 清 十八世纪

name: A Flower Flat Vase — 花口扁瓶
description: This flask-shaped flattened vase from the Qianlong Period period features a mouth with a slight flared shape resembling a plum blossom, a long neck that gently widens to the body, where the belly is adorned with raised lines reminiscent of hanging bells. The foot of the vase flares outward like a plum blossom. The overall shape of the vase is full and rounded. The entire surface is adorned with red and green polychrome enamels. Just below the mouth of the vase is a sculpted Ruyi-shaped collar with famille rose decoration in iron-red enamel. Both sides of the flattened vase have window-like openings decorated with painted scenes depicting narrative stories. On the sides, there are two such window openings on the upper and lower sections, each with depictions of landscapes and floral patterns. The body of the vase is adorned with sculpted pearl-ground motifs and embellished with green enamels. The neck features a design of grapes and squirrels in purple and black enamels. The lower portion of the body is adorned with iron-red Ruyi motifs. The overall polychrome painting is vibrant and the sculpting is lively.
notes: Period as catalogued: Qing Qianlong Period (1736-1795) 清 乾隆（1736 年-1795 年）

name: A Hetian Jade Twin-Dragon Ear Incense Burner — 和田玉夔龙纹双龙耳熏香炉
description: This Hetian white jade incense burner bears resemblance to a similar one in the Forbidden City's Palace Museum collection. The main body is a Ming Dynasty Hetian white jade incense burner, featuring a square shape with a stepped design, larger on top, smaller on the bottom, and geometrically curved in the middle. The front and back of the jade burner are adorned with beast-face and cloud-thunder patterns, while the sides feature twin coiled chi-dragon ears, skillfully crafted in lifelike detail. The lid is made of Qing Dynasty rosewood, intricately carved with a dragon motif and crowned with ancient Han Dynasty jade, which is itself engraved with a pair of Chi dragons. The base, made of Qing Dynasty rosewood, is adorned with relief patterns of spirals and beast faces. Jade's presence dates back to the Neolithic period five thousand years ago, and its development was closely linked to the evolution of production tools. The creation of jade objects primarily involved processes like carving, grinding, engraving, and drilling. Tools made from bone, stone, and quartz sand were used in conjunction with jade production. Archaeological findings reveal the use of tools resembling abrasive wheels in the crafting process. During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, advancements in jade craftsmanship were accelerated by the application of bronze and iron tools, enabling the processing of more intricate designs. The utilization of diamond dust also led to finer surface treatment. In ancient times, Jade artifacts were symbols of imperial and noble status, and their presence was particularly prominent in the imperial courts of the Ming and Qing Dynasties. Similar incense burners can be found in the collections of the Palace Museum in Beijing and the National Palace Museum in Taipei.
notes: Period as catalogued: Ming Dynasty 明代  Material as catalogued: Mixed Media Rosewood Jade

name: Two Hetian Jade Reclining Horses — 和田玉卧马
description: This exquisite piece of Hetian jade features a warm and skillfully carved texture. The jade horse is crafted in a reclining position, with a natural and relaxed demeanor. The horse is depicted with a round carving technique, capturing its form and turning its head to the side in a leisurely manner. The mane is intricately carved in relief, the tail coils to one side, and the smooth lines of its back convey a vivid and lively image. The edges of the entire piece are rounded and polished to perfection, showcasing the craftsmanship's realism and skill in portraying the robust and well-fed physique of the horse. Horses have accompanied human development for a long time, and their significance is reflected in idioms like " Ma Dao Chen Gong " (horses arrive at success) and " Long Ma Jing Shen " (dragon and horse spirit), which highlight their importance. Throughout history, objects related to horses have been highly valued and sought after. References: 1. The Guanfu Museum Collection, Qing Dynasty Qianlong Period period carved white jade reclining horse. 2. "Qianlong Period White Jade Reclining Horse Ornament," Bonhams De Zun Jade Puzhentang Chinese Antique Jade Auction, November 27, 2018.
notes: Period as catalogued: Mid- Qing Dynasty (1736-1850) 清中期（1736 年～ 1850 年）

name: Musician Figures — 陶俑
description: The Musician Figures took a kneeling position, as the female figures wearing headdress, covering with long robes, holding drums and zither. The diverse clothing style of the figures demonstrates the integration of ethnicity on culture and clothing. The tombs contain more than musician figurines but also various other types of figurines, such as guardian figurines, procession figurines, domestic life figurines, animal figurines, and model objects. The discovery of these figurines provides valuable material evidence for studying the social structure, cultural customs, and burial practices of the Northern Wei period, and symbolizes the status and rank of the tomb owner.
notes: Period as catalogued: North Wei 北魏

name: Twain-Handled Jar — 双系罐
description: The Jar with a restrained mouth, two thread shaped handles at both sides, round shoulder, large abdomen, and a flat base. The item is covered entirely with cyan glaze. This type of primary twin-handled jar was covered with a glassy glaze. Besides the glaze's decorative value, it also provided a waterproof quality and made the jars convenient to clean. The glaze would appear in various colors due to the presence of various metallic ions. The glaze for primitive celadon often appeared cyan because it often contained a certain amount of iron protoxide. These kinds of jars were often unearthed in Luoyang, Henan Province. Primary celadon can be traced back to the Shang dynasty, which was three thousand years ago, and it passed through the Zhou, Spring and Autumn, Warring States, and Han periods. It was the transitional product from pottery to porcelain; the inscription technique was developed from pottery-making skills. Celadon made during the Western Zhou era often lacked sophisticated techniques, yet they can be found in larger areas. There was more celadon found in the Yangtze River region than in the Yellow River Delta.
notes: Period as catalogued: West Jin 西晋

name: Autumn Leaf Cup — 秋叶盏
description: The Jizhou Kiln was famous for its black glazed porcelain. According to the public opinion, the history of Jizhou Kiln can be traced back to late Tang, it was famous during the Song era, and declined during the late Yuan era. The Jizhou Kiln was significantly influenced by the "tea competition culture" during the Song period. The "tea competition" was a common activity played by Chinese literati during the song era, and black glazed teacups were deemed as the most prestigious colour in "tea competition". Jizhou Kiln's "muye cup", "daimao cup" and Jian Kiln's "tuhao cup", "youdi glaze", "yaobian glze", and "zheguban cup" are representation of Song black glazed porcelain. The "muye cup"(wooden leaf cup) is one of the most special of its kind, as the leaf inscriptions in the cups were not artificially made, instead, it were the natural shapes of tree leaves. Thus, it made the "muye cup" a rare case in porcelain industry to use natural botanical decorations.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song Dynasty 宋代

name: Jun kiln Washer — 钧窑洗
description: This washer showcases a slanted mouth, slightly curved wall, and short rounded foot. The shape of the carcass was neatly done with straight lining. Yet, its mouth was unbalanced due to the shape shifts made by the burning. The body and foot are covered by gray glaze and the inside is covered with thick glaze and flecks. The Jun Kiln located as the Yuzhou, Henan province, it originates from the North Song era. The most valuable Jun Kiln porcelain were those made during the North era due to the delicate porcelain carcass, and their strong, thick, and muddy glaze. Meanwhile, the colour of Jun Kiln porcelain were purely determined by chance, there was a phrase to describe Jun Kiln porcelain as "same colour before entering kiln and turn out ten thousand colours after burning."
notes: Period as catalogued: Jin Dynasty 金代

name: Large Painted Flower Jar Cizhou Kiln — 磁州窑画花大罐
description: Cizhou Kiln was one of the large kiln in the folk kiln system, the kiln has some distinctive folk kiln features. It played a significant role in the development of Chinese porcelain history. It was recognized as the eight major kiln system during the Song and Yuan period. Cizhou Kiln had profound history as it originates from the Northern Dynasty (386-581), developed during the Sui and Tang era (581-901), and reached its peak during the Song and Yuan era (960-1368). The ancient Cizhou Kiln system spread vastly in Chinese territories, it stretches west from Ningxia to Shandong peninsula, from Mongolia in the north to the lower Yangtze delta in the sounth. The central kiln of Cizhou Kiln was located in the city of Handan, Zhanghe, and Fuyang River's basin. The primary feature of Cizhou Kiln was the use of "da qing clay" as the carcass, then cover the carcass with a layer of white clay to showcase the colour. Thus, the Cizhou Kiln demonstrates the idea of "using delicate works on rough materials." Meanwhile, the white clay was used in various aspects of porcelain making techniques, including incised decorations, carved decorations, ticked decorations, painted decorations, and glazed colours. The Cizhou Kiln adopted the traditional Chinese painting techniques on porcelain, in which created the most exquisite decoration- the "white ground with black flower inscriptions". The strong contrast of Cizhou Kiln's art effect, freedom, unrestrained, and rugged tone reflected the folk custom at that time, and formulated Cizhou Kiln's distinctive folklore identity.
notes: Period as catalogued: Northern Dynasty (386-581)

name: Bronze chariot Axle Cap — 青铜车軎
description: Dimension: Exterior diameter" 9.1cm Length: 8.7 cm The Chariot Axle Cap was made of bronze and was an important part for fixing the wheels, as its inner shape was made round to fit with the wheels. The cap's round exterior wall was inscribed with thunder and cloud decorations, and the column was decorated with dragon figures. The delicate crafting and exquisite decorations on the Chariot Cap suggest it was once owned by an emperor. Chariot Axle Caps are collected in multiple world-famous museums, including the National Palace Museum, National Museum of China, British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Hubei Provincial Museum, and Shaanxi History Museum.
notes: Period as catalogued: Warring States to Early Han 战国时期  Catalogued period spans two dropdown options; the earlier option was selected.

name: A Dragon Robe — 龙袍
description: Dragon robes, also known as gunlongpao (simplified Chinese: 袞龙袍; traditional Chinese: 袞龍袍; pinyin: gǔn lóng páo; hangul: 곤룡포) or longpao for short, is a form of everyday clothing which had a Chinese dragon, called long (龍),as the main decoration; it was worn by the emperors of China. Dragon robes were also adopted by the rulers of neighbouring countries, such as Korea (Goryeo and Joseon dynasties), Vietnam (Nguyễn dynasty), and the Ryukyu Kingdom.The robe supposedly to be the cloth of the empress due to the twain phoenix figures appeared on the dragon robe.
notes: Period as catalogued: Early Qing Dynasty 清代早期  Material as catalogued: Mixed Media (Textiles/Fabric)

name: A Famille Rose Long-Necked Vase — 粉彩长颈瓶
description: Famille rose (French for "pink family") is a type of Chinese porcelain introduced in the 18th century and defined by pink overglaze enamel. It is a Western classification for Qing dynasty porcelain known in Chinese by various terms: fencai, ruancai, yangcai, and falangcai.[1] The colour palette is thought to have been brought to China during the reign of Kangxi (1654–1722) by Western Jesuits who worked at the court. Yet, it was perfected only in the Yongzheng era when the finest pieces were made, and famille rose ware reached the peak of its technical excellence in further era of Qianlong.[2] Famille rose bowl, Imperial porcelain, Jingdezhen. Although famille rose is named after its pink-coloured enamel, the colour may actually range from pale pink to deep ruby. Apart from pink, a range of other soft colour palettes are also used in famille rose. Thegradation of colours was produced by mixing coloured enamels with 'glassy white' (璃白, boli bai), an opaque white enamel (lead arsenate). Its range of colour was further extended by mixing different colours.[3][4] Famille rose was popular in the 18th and 19th century, and it continued to be made in the 20th century. Large quantities of famille rose porcelain were exported to Europe, United States and other countries. Many of these export wares were Jingdezhen porcelain decorated in Canton. Thus, they were known as "Canton famille rose". Besides Famille Rose porcelain that were made in China, many European factories produced such wares as well.
notes: Period as catalogued: the Xianfeng Period of the Qing Dynasty 清代咸丰时期

name: Ding Kiln Gourd-shaped Vase — 宋代定窑葫芦瓶
description: Ding Kiln was the pinnacle of traditional Chinese porcelain industry, and it was also one of the six major kiln system in Song dynasty. Ding Kiln was another porcelain system after Xing Kiln white porcelain which thrived during Tang period. The major production site of Ding Kiln centered around Quyang county in Hebei province. The name Ding for this kiln system was given due to its primary production location as the place was under the administration of Ding state. Ding Kiln was once a folk kiln, it only started to produce for the court after the mid-late Song Dynasty. Ding Kiln originates from Tang, reached its peak during the North Song and Jin dynasty, and ended at Yuan dynasty. It was well known for its white glazed porcelain, yet, Ding Kiln also produce black, caramel, and green glazed porcelain which they were often called "black Ding", "violet Ding", and "green Ding". Ding Kiln came from Xing Kiln, the techniques used for porcelain production received remarkable advancement due to the trajectory of history, shifts of geographical location, and adoption of new materials.
notes: Period as catalogued: Song dynasty 宋代
